title: Who Should Be Baptized?
question: Should infants be baptized, or only people old enough to profess faith?
common: Nearly all Christians agree that Jesus commanded his followers to baptize in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and that baptism marks a person's entry into the life of the church.

views.label: Infants and new believers
views.summary: The Church baptizes infants because baptism is God's free gift of grace, not a reward for understanding. Whole households were baptized in Acts, and Jesus said 'Suffer the little children to come unto me' (Mark 10:14), so parents and godparents bring their children to Christ and promise to raise them in the faith. Adults who come to faith are baptized after a period of preparation.

views.label: Infants fully welcomed
views.summary: Orthodox Christians baptize infants, usually by immersing them three times, and then at once anoint them with holy oil (chrismation) and give them Holy Communion. A child is received into the whole life of the Church from the start, just as a child is born into a family long before it can understand.

views.label: Infants, by God's promise
views.summary: Lutherans baptize infants because baptism is God's work through his Word, not a human decision. The promise is 'unto you, and to your children' (Acts 2:39), and Lutherans hold that the Holy Spirit can create real faith even in a baby, as Luke notes that people brought 'infants' to Jesus for his blessing (Luke 18:15).

views.label: Sign of the covenant
views.summary: Reformed and Presbyterian churches baptize the children of believers as a sign and seal of God's covenant, much as circumcision marked children in Israel. Paul links the two in Colossians 2:11-12. Baptism marks a child as belonging to the covenant community and calls them to lifelong faith, though it does not by itself guarantee salvation.

views.label: Believers only
views.summary: Baptism follows personal faith and repentance: 'Repent, and be baptized' (Acts 2:38). Baptists note that every clear baptism in the New Testament involves people who heard the gospel and believed, like the Ethiopian official (Acts 8:35-38). They usually baptize by full immersion, picturing burial and resurrection with Christ (Romans 6:4).

views.label: A committed adult pledge
views.summary: The Anabaptist movement (Mennonites, Amish, Brethren, Hutterites) began in the 1500s largely over this question. Baptism is 'the answer of a good conscience toward God' (1 Peter 3:21), a public commitment to follow Christ as a disciple within the church, so it is for those old enough to make that commitment freely.

note: Anglicans, Methodists, and most Presbyterians also baptize infants. Many Pentecostal and nondenominational churches practice believer's baptism.

title: What Baptism Does
question: Is baptism a means by which God saves, or a public sign of salvation already received?
common: Christians agree that baptism is commanded by Christ, is tied to repentance and new life, and pictures union with Christ in his death and resurrection (Romans 6:3-4).

views.label: Cleansing and new birth
views.summary: Baptism truly removes original sin and all personal sin and gives new birth as a child of God through the Holy Spirit. Catholics read Jesus' words about being 'born of water and of the Spirit' (John 3:5) and Peter's statement that 'baptism doth also now save us' (1 Peter 3:21) as describing what baptism really does. God is not bound by the sacraments, so the Church also recognizes that some can be saved without water baptism, such as those who die for Christ or who desire baptism but die before receiving it.

views.label: Dying and rising with Christ
views.summary: Baptism is a real dying and rising with Christ in which a person is cleansed, born anew, and joined to his body, the Church. It is followed immediately by chrismation, the seal of the gift of the Holy Spirit. The Orthodox see it as the beginning of a lifelong path of healing and transformation.

views.label: God's Word with the water
views.summary: Baptism is not plain water but water joined to God's command and promise. Through it God forgives sins, rescues from death and the devil, and gives eternal salvation to all who believe, as Jesus said: 'He that believeth and is baptized shall be saved' (Mark 16:16). It is God's action received by faith, and Christians return to it daily in repentance.

views.label: Sign and seal of grace
views.summary: Baptism is a sign and seal of the covenant of grace, a visible promise that God washes away sin through Christ. The Holy Spirit uses it to confirm and strengthen faith, but grace is not tied to the moment of baptism and the outward washing does not save by itself. Peter himself says it is 'not the putting away of the filth of the flesh, but the answer of a good conscience toward God' (1 Peter 3:21).

views.label: An act of obedience
views.summary: Baptism is an ordinance, an act of obedience that publicly shows a salvation already received by grace through faith (Ephesians 2:8-9). It is a real and important picture of union with Christ, but it does not cause that union. Baptists often point out that the thief on the cross was promised paradise without being baptized (Luke 23:42-43).

note: Anglicans and Methodists describe baptism as a sacrament and means of grace, with a range of emphases. Churches of Christ teach that baptism of believers is the moment God forgives sins (Acts 2:38).

title: The Lord's Supper
question: How is Christ present in the bread and the cup?
common: All Christians celebrate the meal Jesus gave on the night before he died. They agree that it proclaims his death 'till he come' (1 Corinthians 11:26) and unites believers with him and with one another.

views.label: Truly his Body and Blood
views.summary: At the consecration, the bread and wine become the true Body and Blood of Christ, while still looking and tasting like bread and wine. The Church calls this change transubstantiation. Catholics take Jesus' words 'This is my body' and his teaching that 'my flesh is meat indeed' (John 6:55) at face value. The Mass makes present Christ's one sacrifice on the cross; it does not repeat it.

views.label: A holy mystery
views.summary: The Orthodox firmly believe the bread and wine truly become the Body and Blood of Christ, through the prayer that calls down the Holy Spirit on the gifts. They generally prefer not to define exactly how this happens, receiving it as a mystery with faith and awe. Paul calls the cup and bread 'the communion of the blood of Christ' and 'of the body of Christ' (1 Corinthians 10:16).

views.label: In, with, and under
views.summary: Christ's true Body and Blood are present 'in, with, and under' the bread and wine, given for the forgiveness of sins. Lutherans hold to the plain words 'This is my body' rather than treating them as a symbol, but they do not teach that the bread stops being bread, and they do not attempt to explain how. Many Lutherans reject the label 'consubstantiation' sometimes applied to their view.

views.label: Real spiritual presence
views.summary: Christ is truly present and truly received, but spiritually, by the power of the Holy Spirit, rather than locally in the bread and wine. Christ's body is in heaven, and believers who eat in faith are lifted up to feed on him there. The Supper is a real 'communion' with Christ (1 Corinthians 10:16), not a bare reminder.

views.label: A memorial meal
views.summary: The Lord's Supper is an ordinance in which believers remember Christ's death, as he said: 'this do in remembrance of me' (Luke 22:19). The bread and cup are symbols, and Christ is present by his Spirit among his gathered people rather than in the elements. This view is often traced to the Swiss reformer Ulrich Zwingli.

note: Anglicans and Methodists affirm Christ's real presence but describe it in a range of ways, from close to the Reformed view to close to the Catholic and Orthodox view.

title: Election and Predestination
question: Does God choose who will be saved, and on what basis?
common: All Christians affirm that God is sovereign, that salvation is his gracious gift and not earned, and that the Bible speaks of believers as 'elect' and 'predestinated.' They differ on how God's choosing relates to human response.

views.label: Unconditional election
views.summary: Before the creation of the world, God freely chose a people for salvation in Christ, not because of foreseen faith or works but 'according to the good pleasure of his will' (Ephesians 1:5). Romans 9 says God's choice is 'not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy' (Romans 9:16). Those God chooses he surely calls, justifies, and glorifies (Romans 8:30).

views.label: Election by foreknowledge
views.summary: God 'will have all men to be saved' (1 Timothy 2:4) and by grace enables every person to respond to the gospel. Predestination rests on God's foreknowledge: 'whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate' (Romans 8:29). Many Wesleyans read Romans 9 as speaking of God's purposes for peoples and nations in history, and Ephesians 1 as the choosing of a people 'in him,' that is, all who are in Christ.

views.label: Chosen by grace alone
views.summary: Everyone who is saved is saved entirely by God's gracious choice, and this truth is meant to comfort believers. But Lutherans do not teach that God chose anyone for damnation, since he sincerely wants all to be saved; those who are lost resist his grace. Lutherans hold both truths without building a system to reconcile them.

views.label: Grace first, real freedom
views.summary: God's eternal plan includes predestination, and every good response to him begins with his grace. Yet people truly cooperate with grace or refuse it, and God predestines no one to hell. Catholic theologians, such as the Thomists and Molinists, have long debated how this works, and the Church permits a range of views within these limits.

views.label: Foreknowledge and cooperation
views.summary: The Orthodox read predestination in light of God's foreknowledge (Romans 8:29) and his love for all people. Salvation is a cooperation, or synergy, between God's grace and human freedom, with grace always leading. The Orthodox generally have not developed detailed teachings on predestination like those of the Western churches.

note: Baptists and other evangelicals are divided on this question: some hold the Reformed view, while many others hold a view close to the Wesleyan one.

title: Free Will and Grace
question: Can a person choose God, or must God first change the heart?
common: Christians agree that sin has deeply damaged human nature, that no one can save themselves, and that God's grace must take the first step.

views.label: Grace renews the will
views.summary: Sinners are 'dead in trespasses and sins' (Ephesians 2:1) and cannot choose God until he gives them new life. God's saving grace is effective: it does not force people against their will but renews the will so they freely come to Christ, as when the Lord 'opened' Lydia's heart (Acts 16:14). Jesus said no one can come to him unless the Father draws him (John 6:44).

views.label: Grace that goes before
views.summary: God's 'prevenient' grace goes before every person, waking the conscience and freeing the will enough to respond to him. Because 'the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men' (Titus 2:11), everyone can accept or refuse Christ. Salvation is entirely by grace, yet that grace can be resisted.

views.label: Bound will, resistible grace
views.summary: In spiritual matters the fallen will is bound and cannot turn to God on its own, as Luther argued in The Bondage of the Will. Faith is entirely God's gift, created by the Holy Spirit through the Word and sacraments. Yet people can resist and reject that grace, so those who are lost bear the blame themselves.

views.label: Grace and cooperation
views.summary: No one can turn to God without his grace, which always comes first. Grace heals and frees the will so a person can truly cooperate with it. Paul holds both sides together: 'work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do' (Philippians 2:12-13).

views.label: Synergy with God
views.summary: Human freedom, though wounded by sin, is not destroyed. Salvation comes through synergy, God and the person working together, with God's grace always taking the lead. Christ stands at the door and knocks, and the person opens (Revelation 3:20).

note: Many Baptists, Pentecostals, and other evangelicals hold views close to either the Reformed or the Wesleyan position.

title: Can Salvation Be Lost?
question: Can someone who truly believes fall away and be lost?
common: Christians agree that God is faithful, that believers are kept by his power, and that Scripture gives serious warnings against turning away from Christ.

views.label: God keeps his own
views.summary: Those God truly saves he will keep to the end; no one can pluck them out of the Father's hand (John 10:28-29), and he who began a good work will finish it (Philippians 1:6). The warnings in Hebrews are real means God uses to keep his people, or they describe people who were never truly converted, as 1 John 2:19 says of those who 'went out from us.'

views.label: Eternal security
views.summary: A person who has been born again cannot become unborn. Salvation rests on Christ's finished work, not on the believer's ongoing performance, and nothing 'shall be able to separate us from the love of God' (Romans 8:38-39). Believers who sin face God's loving discipline, but not the loss of salvation.

views.label: Faith can be abandoned
views.summary: True believers can, through persistent and willful sin or unbelief, turn away from grace and be lost. Wesleyans read Hebrews 6 and Jesus' words about branches that are cut off from the vine (John 15:6) as real warnings to real believers. Most also teach that those who fall away can be restored if they return in repentance.

views.label: Faith can be lost
views.summary: Lutherans teach that God's elect will certainly be saved, yet they also teach that a believer can lose faith and the Holy Spirit through unbelief or deliberate sin. They hold both truths, as Scripture states them, without a system to reconcile them, and point troubled believers back to God's promise.

views.label: Lost and restored
views.summary: A baptized person can lose sanctifying grace through mortal sin, a grave sin committed with full knowledge and deliberate consent. That grace can be restored through repentance and the sacrament of Reconciliation. Perseverance to the end is itself a gift of God, to be prayed for with hope: 'he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved' (Matthew 24:13).

views.label: A path one can leave
views.summary: Salvation is a lifelong journey of union with God, not only a single past event. A person can turn away from God by free choice, and can return through repentance, as the prodigal son did (Luke 15:24). The Orthodox stress watchfulness and perseverance to the end.

note: Free Will Baptists and some other Baptists hold that a believer can fall away, so not all Baptists hold eternal security.

title: Faith and Works
question: Are we made right with God by faith alone, or by faith working through love?
common: All Christians agree that salvation is a gift of God's grace through Jesus Christ, that no one can earn it, and that true faith shows itself in good works. In 1999 Catholic and Lutheran leaders signed a joint statement affirming a shared basic understanding of justification by grace, while noting differences that remain.

views.label: By faith alone
views.summary: We are declared righteous before God by grace alone through faith alone, for Christ's sake, 'without the deeds of the law' (Romans 3:28). Christ's righteousness is credited to the believer, as faith was 'counted unto him for righteousness' with Abraham (Romans 4:3-5). Good works necessarily follow as the fruit of faith but add nothing to justification; James is read as teaching that living faith is never without works.

views.label: Faith alone, never alone
views.summary: Justification is God's legal declaration that a sinner is righteous because Christ's obedience is credited to them, received by faith alone. Reformed Christians often say, following Calvin, that faith alone justifies, but the faith that justifies is never alone. James shows that real faith is proved by its works: 'I will shew thee my faith by my works' (James 2:18).

views.label: Grace that makes righteous
views.summary: Justification is a free gift no one can merit, received by faith and baptism. It does not only declare a person righteous but truly makes them righteous within, as 'the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost' (Romans 5:5). Catholics note that James says 'by works a man is justified, and not by faith only' (James 2:24) and that Paul speaks of 'faith which worketh by love' (Galatians 5:6); the 'works' Paul rejects are works done to earn God's favor.

views.label: Salvation as healing
views.summary: The Orthodox usually describe salvation less in courtroom terms and more as healing and union with God. Faith and works are not rivals; faith is living trust that shows itself in love, prayer, and repentance. Paul and James are seen as describing the same living faith from two sides.

views.label: Faith alone, then holiness
views.summary: Wesleyans affirm justification by grace through faith alone, as their Articles of Religion state. They put strong weight on what follows: the new birth and a life of growing holiness, since 'faith, if it hath not works, is dead' (James 2:17).

note: The Anglican Thirty-nine Articles also teach that we are justified 'by Faith only' (Article XI); several other church bodies, including Methodists, later affirmed the 1999 joint statement.

title: Israel and the Church
question: Does God still have a distinct plan for ethnic Israel?
common: Christians agree that God made real promises to Abraham and Israel, that Jesus is Israel's Messiah, and that Jews and Gentiles alike are saved through him. Christians of every tradition reject hatred of the Jewish people.

views.label: God's gifts are irrevocable
views.summary: The Church is the new People of God, yet the Jewish people remain dear to God, 'for the gifts and calling of God are without repentance' (Romans 11:29). Since the Second Vatican Council, Catholic teaching has stressed this ongoing bond and rejected any idea that Jews as a people are guilty of Christ's death. Catholics also look toward a future in which 'all Israel' will recognize the Messiah (Romans 11:26).

views.label: The Church fulfills Israel
views.summary: The Orthodox see the Church as the continuation and fulfillment of Israel, 'the Israel of God' (Galatians 6:16), made up of Jews and Gentiles in one body. Many Orthodox writers, following the church fathers, also expect the Jewish people to turn to Christ before the end.

views.label: One people of God
views.summary: God has one people across history, gathered under one covenant of grace. Gentile believers are grafted into the same olive tree as faithful Israel (Romans 11:17), and all who belong to Christ are 'Abraham's seed' (Galatians 3:29). Many Reformed interpreters expect a large future turning of Jewish people to Christ, based on Romans 11:25-26, while others read 'all Israel' as the whole number of God's people.

views.label: A distinct future for Israel
views.summary: God's promises to ethnic Israel, including the land and a restored kingdom, will be fulfilled as the prophets foretold (Ezekiel 37:21-28). The church is a distinct people formed at Pentecost and does not replace Israel. After 'the fulness of the Gentiles be come in,' God will turn again to Israel as a nation (Romans 11:25-26).

note: Views vary within most traditions. Labels such as 'covenant theology,' 'dispensationalism,' and 'replacement' or 'fulfillment' theology are often used in this debate, and each side defines them differently.

title: The Thousand Years
question: What is the thousand-year reign in Revelation 20?
common: Christians agree that Christ will return in glory, raise the dead, judge the world, and make all things new.

views.label: Christ reigns now
views.summary: Following St. Augustine, the Church understands the thousand years as a symbol of the present age, in which Christ reigns through his Church and Satan's power is restrained. The Church has rejected the idea of an earthly political kingdom of Christ before the final judgment, and expects one glorious return followed by the resurrection and judgment.

views.label: The reign is now
views.summary: The Orthodox read the thousand years as the present life of the Church, in which Christ already reigns and the saints share in his victory. They expect one return of Christ, followed by the general resurrection and judgment. The Creed confesses that his 'kingdom shall have no end' (compare Luke 1:33).

views.label: Amillennial
views.summary: Revelation 20 describes the whole age between Christ's first and second comings. Satan is 'bound' in that he cannot stop the gospel from reaching the nations, as Jesus spoke of binding the strong man (Matthew 12:29), and believers who have died reign with Christ in heaven. Christ's single return will bring the resurrection, judgment, and new creation.

views.label: Postmillennial
views.summary: Postmillennialists believe the gospel will gradually win most of the world, bringing a long era of righteousness and peace before Christ returns. They point to the parables of the mustard seed and the leaven (Matthew 13:31-33) and the promise that 'the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD' (Habakkuk 2:14). This view was common among the Puritans and many evangelicals of the 1800s.

views.label: Premillennial
views.summary: Christ will return before a literal thousand-year reign on earth, when he will rule the nations and Satan will be bound. Premillennialists point to the two resurrections in Revelation 20:4-6 and note that early Christian writers such as Justin Martyr and Irenaeus held this view. Dispensationalists see this kingdom as fulfilling God's promises to national Israel, while 'historic premillennialists' do not draw that distinction.

note: Views on the millennium often cut across denominations, and many churches allow members to hold any of these views.

title: The Rapture and the Tribulation
question: Will believers be caught up before a time of great tribulation?
common: Christians agree that Christ will return visibly, that 'the dead in Christ shall rise,' and that living believers will be 'caught up' to meet the Lord (1 Thessalonians 4:16-17).

views.label: Pre-tribulation rapture
views.summary: Christ will come for his church in a 'rapture' before a seven-year tribulation, then return with his saints at its end to set up his kingdom. Supporters point to the promise that 'God hath not appointed us to wrath' (1 Thessalonians 5:9) and that believers will be kept 'from the hour of temptation' (Revelation 3:10). The tribulation is seen as Daniel's seventieth week, focused on Israel (Daniel 9:27).

views.label: Post-tribulation rapture
views.summary: The church will go through the tribulation and be caught up when Christ returns at its end. Jesus places the gathering of his elect 'after the tribulation of those days' (Matthew 24:29-31). The word 'meet' in 1 Thessalonians 4:17 was used for citizens going out to welcome a visiting king and escort him back to their city, which suggests believers rise to greet Christ as he comes to earth.

views.label: One glorious return
views.summary: The Church teaches one return of Christ in glory at the end of history, when the dead will be raised and all will be judged. Being 'caught up' in 1 Thessalonians 4 is part of that one coming, not a separate, earlier event. The Church does expect a final trial before Christ comes that will shake the faith of many believers.

views.label: A single Second Coming
views.summary: These churches teach a single, visible Second Coming at the end of the age. Paul's description of being 'caught up' is read as believers rising to meet the Lord as he comes to judge and renew the world, not a departure years earlier. Many in these traditions read Matthew 24 as speaking partly of Jerusalem's fall in AD 70 and partly of the final end.

note: Other views include a mid-tribulation rapture and a 'pre-wrath' rapture. Many Baptist and Pentecostal churches hold the pre-tribulation view, though not all do.

title: Spiritual Gifts Today
question: Are gifts like prophecy, tongues, and healing still given today?
common: Christians agree that the Holy Spirit gives every believer gifts to build up the church, and that love is greater than any gift (1 Corinthians 13:13).

views.label: All the gifts continue
views.summary: All the gifts listed in 1 Corinthians 12, including tongues, prophecy, and healing, are for the church today, since the promise of Pentecost is 'to all that are afar off' (Acts 2:39). Pentecostals read 'when that which is perfect is come' (1 Corinthians 13:10) as Christ's return, so the gifts continue until then. Paul's call to 'covet earnestly the best gifts' (1 Corinthians 12:31) still applies.

views.label: Sign gifts have ceased
views.summary: Cessationists believe the miraculous 'sign gifts,' such as tongues, prophecy, and healing at an apostle's word, confirmed the apostles' message while the New Testament was being given. The church is 'built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets' (Ephesians 2:20), a foundation laid once. God still heals and works wonders in answer to prayer, but not through those gifts as they worked in the apostolic age.

views.label: Open but cautious
views.summary: Many evangelicals hold that Scripture does not clearly say the miraculous gifts have ended, but they are careful about claims today. They test prophecy by Scripture ('Despise not prophesyings. Prove all things,' 1 Thessalonians 5:20-21) and stress Paul's call that 'all things be done decently and in order' (1 Corinthians 14:40).

views.label: Charisms continue, discerned
views.summary: The Holy Spirit still gives charisms, both ordinary and extraordinary, for building up the Church. They are to be received with gratitude and tested by the Church's pastors. The Catholic Charismatic Renewal, which began in 1967, is a recognized movement in the Church, and the Church investigates reported miracles carefully.

views.label: Gifts within the Church's life
views.summary: The Holy Spirit continues to work wonders, especially through the saints and holy elders. The Orthodox honor these gifts but are wary of seeking spiritual experiences for their own sake, stressing humility, repentance, and prayer as the path of life in the Spirit.

title: Speaking in Tongues
question: What is speaking in tongues, and is it meant for every believer?
common: Christians agree that at Pentecost the disciples were filled with the Holy Spirit and spoke so that people from many nations heard God's works in their own languages (Acts 2:6-11).

views.label: Sign of Spirit baptism
views.summary: Classical Pentecostal churches, such as the Assemblies of God, teach that speaking in tongues is the first physical sign of being baptized in the Holy Spirit, following the pattern of Acts 2, 10, and 19. Tongues may be a real human language or a language of prayer in the spirit (1 Corinthians 14:2, 14). Believers are encouraged to seek this gift.

views.label: A gift, not for all
views.summary: Charismatics in many denominations welcome tongues as a real and valuable gift for prayer and worship but do not see it as the required sign of the Spirit's presence. Paul asks, 'do all speak with tongues?' (1 Corinthians 12:30), expecting the answer no.

views.label: A founding-era gift
views.summary: Biblical tongues were real, unlearned human languages, as at Pentecost, given as a sign while the church was being founded. Many in these churches believe that gift ended with the apostolic age, and that modern experiences, however sincere, are not the same gift.

views.label: A charism among many
views.summary: The Church recognizes tongues as a genuine gift the Spirit may give, while teaching that it is not required for salvation and is not a measure of holiness. Paul's guidelines for order and interpretation in worship (1 Corinthians 14:27-28) apply.

views.label: The gospel in every language
views.summary: Many Orthodox teachers see the Pentecost gift of languages as a sign that the gospel is for every nation, reversing the confusion of Babel (Genesis 11:7-9). It is fulfilled as the Church worships in the languages of each people. Speaking in tongues is not part of Orthodox worship or devotional practice.

title: Women in Church Leadership
question: May women serve as pastors, priests, or elders?
common: Christians agree that men and women are equally made in God's image, equally redeemed in Christ, and called to serve. Women such as Phoebe and Priscilla served the early church (Romans 16:1-3).

views.label: Priesthood reserved to men
views.summary: The Church teaches that it has no authority to ordain women as priests, because Christ chose only men as his twelve apostles, and the priest represents Christ the Bridegroom. This is understood as a matter of the Church's nature, not of women's worth. Women serve in many vital ways, and Mary, the greatest of the saints, was not given the apostles' office.

views.label: Priesthood reserved to men
views.summary: The Orthodox Church ordains only men to the priesthood, following Christ's example and the Church's unbroken practice. The early church had women deacons, such as Phoebe, 'a servant of the church' (Romans 16:1), and some Orthodox churches have discussed restoring that order.

views.tradition: Many Baptists, Reformed, and other evangelicals
views.label: Pastors and elders are men
views.summary: Complementarians believe men and women are equal in worth but given different roles. They read 'I suffer not a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority over the man' (1 Timothy 2:12) as a lasting rule, since Paul grounds it in creation, not local culture (1 Timothy 2:13). Women serve widely, but the office of pastor or elder is for qualified men.

views.tradition: Many Methodists, Pentecostals, Anglicans, and Lutherans
views.label: All roles open to women
views.summary: Egalitarians believe the Spirit gives gifts of leadership to women and men alike, since in Christ 'there is neither male nor female' (Galatians 3:28) and the Spirit was poured out so that 'your sons and your daughters shall prophesy' (Acts 2:17). They read 1 Timothy 2 and 1 Corinthians 14 as answers to specific problems in those churches. They point to Deborah, who judged Israel (Judges 4:4), and Priscilla, who taught Apollos (Acts 18:26).

note: Many denominations are divided on this question; some Lutheran, Anglican, Pentecostal, and Baptist bodies ordain women, while others in the same families do not.

title: Mary, the Mother of Jesus
question: What honor belongs to Mary, the mother of Jesus?
common: Christians agree that Mary was a virgin when she conceived Jesus by the Holy Spirit, that she is a model of faith ('be it unto me according to thy word,' Luke 1:38), and that 'all generations shall call me blessed' (Luke 1:48).

views.label: Mother of God, sinless
views.summary: Mary is the Mother of God because her son is God. Catholics believe she was preserved from original sin from her conception (the Immaculate Conception), remained ever-virgin, and was taken body and soul into heaven (the Assumption). The angel's greeting, which Catholic tradition renders 'full of grace' (Luke 1:28), and Jesus' words from the cross (John 19:26-27) ground her role as spiritual mother of believers, who honor her and ask her prayers, while worship belongs to God alone.

views.label: Theotokos, all-holy
views.summary: The Orthodox honor Mary as Theotokos, 'God-bearer,' a title confirmed at the Council of Ephesus in 431 to protect the truth that Jesus is fully God. She is ever-virgin and praised as 'more honorable than the cherubim,' and the Church celebrates her falling asleep (the Dormition) and her being taken into heaven. The Orthodox do not use the Catholic teaching of the Immaculate Conception, but they hold her as all-holy.

views.label: Honored model of faith
views.summary: Lutherans affirm the ancient title 'Mother of God' and honor Mary as the greatest example of receiving God's grace by faith. Luther wrote warmly about her song, the Magnificat, and the Lutheran Confessions call her 'ever virgin,' though not all Lutherans today hold that view. Lutherans do not pray to Mary or teach the Immaculate Conception or the Assumption as doctrine, since they find no clear basis for them in Scripture.

views.label: Blessed, faithful servant
views.summary: Evangelicals honor Mary as a godly woman chosen by grace, whose song 'my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour' (Luke 1:47) shows that she too rejoiced in God's salvation. Most believe Mary and Joseph had other children after Jesus, the brothers and sisters named in Matthew 13:55-56. They do not pray to Mary, holding that there is 'one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus' (1 Timothy 2:5).

note: Catholics and Orthodox understand Jesus' 'brethren' as close relatives such as cousins, or as Joseph's children from an earlier marriage. Anglican views of Mary range from close to the evangelical view to close to the Catholic view.

title: Peter and Church Authority
question: What did Jesus give Peter, and does it continue in the church today?
common: Christians agree that Peter was a leading apostle, that Christ himself is the church's true foundation (1 Corinthians 3:11), and that Jesus promised 'the gates of hell shall not prevail' against his church (Matthew 16:18).

views.label: Peter's office continues
views.summary: Jesus renamed Simon 'Peter,' meaning rock, said he would build his church on this rock, and gave him 'the keys of the kingdom of heaven' (Matthew 16:18-19), echoing the royal steward's key in Isaiah 22:22. He later charged Peter to 'Feed my sheep' (John 21:17). Catholics believe this office continues in the bishops of Rome, Peter's successors, as a visible source of unity for the whole Church; under strict conditions, the pope can define teaching on faith and morals without error.

views.label: First among equals
views.summary: The Orthodox honor Peter as chief of the apostles and recognize that the bishop of Rome held a primacy of honor in the early church. But the power to bind and loose was given to all the apostles (Matthew 18:18), and the 'rock' is the faith Peter confessed, shared by every faithful bishop. The church is guided by bishops together in councils, as in Acts 15, rather than by one bishop over all.

views.label: The rock is the confession
views.summary: Many Protestants read the 'rock' as Peter's confession that Jesus is 'the Christ, the Son of the living God' (Matthew 16:16); others see Peter himself in his unique, unrepeatable role as a founding apostle. The keys are the preaching of the gospel and church discipline, given to the church (Matthew 18:18). Authority today rests on the apostles' teaching recorded in Scripture, the church's foundation (Ephesians 2:20).

note: Anglicans honor Peter and keep bishops in historic succession, but do not accept the pope's authority over their churches.

title: Scripture and Tradition
question: Is the Bible the only final authority, or does it come together with the church's tradition?
common: Christians agree that Scripture is 'given by inspiration of God' (2 Timothy 3:16) and that the faith was handed down from the apostles.

views.label: Scripture and Tradition together
views.summary: God's revelation comes through both Sacred Scripture and Sacred Tradition, which flow from the same source, and the Church's teaching office (the Magisterium) interprets them. Paul told believers to 'hold the traditions which ye have been taught, whether by word, or our epistle' (2 Thessalonians 2:15), and calls the church 'the pillar and ground of the truth' (1 Timothy 3:15). The Magisterium is not above God's Word but serves it.

views.label: Scripture within Holy Tradition
views.summary: Scripture is the heart of Holy Tradition, the living memory of the Holy Spirit in the Church, which also includes the creeds, the councils, the church fathers, the liturgy, and the icons. Scripture is read rightly within the Church that recognized and preserved it.

views.label: Scripture alone is final
views.summary: Scripture alone is the final, supreme rule for faith and life, because it alone is God-breathed (2 Timothy 3:16). Creeds, councils, and church tradition are valued as helpful guides, but they can err and must be tested by Scripture. Jesus warned against 'making the word of God of none effect through your tradition' (Mark 7:13).

views.label: Scripture first, with tradition, reason
views.summary: Anglicans hold that Scripture 'containeth all things necessary to salvation' (Article VI), while giving real weight to the creeds, the early church, and reason in interpreting it. This is often pictured as a three-legged stool on which Scripture carries the most weight.

views.label: Scripture first, with three guides
views.summary: Methodists treat Scripture as the primary source of Christian teaching, read with the help of tradition, reason, and Christian experience, a pattern often called the 'Wesleyan quadrilateral.' John Wesley called himself 'a man of one book' while drawing deeply on the early church.

note: Many Baptists, Pentecostals, and other evangelicals also hold to Scripture alone, often placing especially strong weight on each believer reading the Bible for themselves.

title: The Days of Creation
question: Were the days of Genesis 1 ordinary days, and how old is the earth?
common: Christians agree that God created everything out of nothing, that creation is good, and that human beings are made in God's image (Genesis 1:27).

views.label: Six days, young earth
views.summary: Young-earth creationists read the days as six ordinary days, since each has 'the evening and the morning' and Exodus 20:11 bases the weekly Sabbath on them. The genealogies in Genesis point to an earth thousands, not billions, of years old. They see this as the plain reading, and hold that death entered the world through Adam's sin (Romans 5:12).

views.tradition: Many Reformed, Anglican, and other evangelicals
views.label: Old earth, true history
views.summary: Many conservative Protestants accept an old earth while holding Genesis as true. Some read each 'day' as a long age, since the Hebrew word can mean a period of time ('in the day that the LORD God made the earth and the heavens,' Genesis 2:4), while others read the days as a literary framework that arranges God's work by theme. They note that 'one day is with the Lord as a thousand years' (2 Peter 3:8).

views.label: True teaching, open on science
views.summary: The Church teaches that God created all things from nothing and that Genesis tells true things about God, humanity, and sin, often using figurative language. Catholics are free to accept scientific findings about the age of the earth and the development of life, provided they hold that God directly creates each human soul and that humanity truly fell. Faith and reason come from the same God and cannot truly conflict.

views.label: Read with the fathers
views.summary: The Orthodox read Genesis with the church fathers, such as St. Basil, who drew deep spiritual and theological meaning from the six days. Some Orthodox hold to a young earth, while others accept modern science, and the Church has made no formal ruling on the age of the earth.

note: Views on this question cut across denominations more than most, and Christians who agree on nearly everything else may differ here.

title: Hell and Final Judgment
question: What is hell, and is it everlasting conscious punishment?
common: Christians agree that God is both just and loving, that there will be a final judgment, and that Jesus spoke seriously and often about the danger of being lost.

views.label: Eternal separation from God
views.summary: Hell is the state of definitive self-exclusion from communion with God, freely chosen by those who die in grave sin without repentance. Its chief pain is eternal separation from God, for whom we were made. The Church teaches that hell is eternal (Matthew 25:46), that God predestines no one to go there, and it has never declared that any particular person is in hell.

views.label: God's love experienced as fire
views.summary: Many Orthodox teachers describe heaven and hell as two ways of experiencing the same presence of God: to those who love him, his glory is light and joy, while to those who reject him it is like a burning fire, for 'our God is a consuming fire' (Hebrews 12:29). The Church affirms eternal judgment while praying for the salvation of all. A few Orthodox thinkers have hoped that all might finally be saved, but the Church has not taught this as doctrine.

views.tradition: Most Lutheran, Reformed, Baptist, and Pentecostal churches
views.label: Everlasting conscious punishment
views.summary: Those who reject God will experience conscious punishment forever. Jesus used the same word, 'everlasting,' for both punishment and life in Matthew 25:46, and Revelation speaks of torment with 'no rest day nor night' (Revelation 14:11). This has been the majority view through church history.

views.label: Final destruction
views.summary: Some evangelicals, including the Anglican leader John Stott, have held that the lost will finally be destroyed rather than suffer forever, a view called conditional immortality or annihilationism. Scripture often speaks of the wicked 'perishing' and being destroyed 'both soul and body' (Matthew 10:28), and calls the lake of fire 'the second death' (Revelation 20:14). On this view the punishment is everlasting in its result, not in its experience.

note: A small number of Christians in several traditions hope or hold that all people will finally be saved; no major church body teaches this as doctrine.

title: How the Cross Saves
question: How does Jesus' death save us?
common: Christians agree that 'Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures' (1 Corinthians 15:3) and rose again, and that the cross reveals God's love. Most traditions use several biblical pictures together: sacrifice, ransom, victory, and example.

views.label: Christ bore our penalty
views.summary: Christ bore the penalty for sin in the place of sinners, satisfying God's justice so that God is 'just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus' (Romans 3:26). Isaiah says 'the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all' (Isaiah 53:6), and Paul says God 'made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin' (2 Corinthians 5:21). Many Lutherans, Baptists, and other evangelicals share this emphasis, often called penal substitution.

views.label: A sacrifice of perfect love
views.summary: Christ's death is a sacrifice of perfect love and obedience offered to the Father, which makes satisfaction for sins and reconciles humanity to God. Catholics, drawing on St. Anselm and St. Thomas Aquinas, stress that Christ freely gave his life 'a ransom for many' (Mark 10:45). Believers are invited to unite their own sufferings with his (Colossians 1:24).

views.label: Victory over death
views.summary: By his death Christ entered death itself and broke its power, freeing humanity from the devil and from corruption (Hebrews 2:14-15). The Easter hymn proclaims, 'Christ is risen from the dead, trampling down death by death.' The Orthodox also use sacrificial language, but many of their teachers are uneasy with describing the cross mainly as the Father punishing the Son.

views.label: Sacrifice for the whole world
views.summary: Christ died as a sacrifice for sin, not for some only but for 'the sins of the whole world' (1 John 2:2), so salvation is truly offered to everyone. Wesleyans hold together Christ's substitution for sinners and the power of the cross to heal and make people holy.

note: Christians also differ on whether Christ died to secure the salvation of the elect in particular, a view held by many Reformed believers, or for every person equally, as most other traditions hold.

title: Sabbath and the Lord's Day
question: Should Christians keep the Sabbath, and on which day?
common: Christians agree that God gave rest as a gift, that 'the Son of man is Lord also of the sabbath' (Mark 2:28), and that from the earliest days believers gathered on the first day of the week, the day of the resurrection (Acts 20:7).

views.label: Sunday, the Lord's Day
views.summary: Sunday, the day of Christ's resurrection, fulfills the Sabbath and is 'the Lord's day' (Revelation 1:10). Catholics are obliged to take part in Mass on Sundays and holy days and to avoid work that hinders worship and rest. The Sabbath command is kept by honoring the Lord's Day.

views.label: Sunday, the eighth day
views.summary: Every Sunday is a 'little Easter,' sometimes called the eighth day, the first day of the new creation. The Orthodox still honor Saturday as the Sabbath with special remembrance of the departed, but Sunday is the chief day of worship.

views.label: The Christian Sabbath
views.summary: Many Reformed and Presbyterian churches teach that the fourth commandment belongs to God's lasting moral law, since the Sabbath was made at creation, before Moses (Genesis 2:3). Since the resurrection it is kept on Sunday as the Christian Sabbath, a whole day set apart for worship, rest, and works of mercy, as the Westminster Confession teaches.

views.label: Freedom, with weekly worship
views.summary: Keeping a particular day was part of the ceremonial law fulfilled in Christ, 'a shadow of things to come' (Colossians 2:16-17). The heart of the commandment, as Luther's Small Catechism explains, is not to despise preaching and God's Word but to hold it sacred and gladly hear and learn it, which is why the church gathers on Sunday.

note: Seventh-day Adventists and Seventh Day Baptists keep Saturday as the Sabbath, holding that the commandment's seventh day was never changed. Baptists and other evangelicals hold a range of the views above.

title: Tithing
question: Are Christians required to give a tenth of their income?
common: Christians agree that everything belongs to God, that giving is an act of worship, and that 'God loveth a cheerful giver' (2 Corinthians 9:7).

views.tradition: Many Baptists, Pentecostals, and other evangelicals
views.label: The tithe as a baseline
views.summary: Many evangelicals teach the tithe, a tenth of income, as the starting point for Christian giving. Tithing came before the law of Moses, when Abraham gave a tenth to Melchizedek (Genesis 14:20), and Jesus affirmed it while stressing justice and mercy: 'these ought ye to have done' (Matthew 23:23). Malachi 3:10 is read as God's invitation to trust him.

views.tradition: Many Lutheran, Reformed, and other Protestants
views.label: Generous, proportional giving
views.summary: The tithe belonged to Israel's law, where it supported the Levites and the temple. The New Testament does not command a tenth but calls believers to give regularly 'as God hath prospered him' (1 Corinthians 16:2), freely and generously. Many still see a tenth as a helpful guide.

views.label: Support the Church as able
views.summary: One of the precepts of the Church asks Catholics to help provide for the Church's needs, each according to their ability. The Church does not require a fixed tenth, though some parishes encourage tithing, and it gives special weight to almsgiving to the poor.

views.label: Giving as part of devotion
views.summary: Giving is joined with prayer and fasting as part of the Christian life. There is no single binding rule on the amount, though many Orthodox parishes encourage the tithe as a goal and practice regular stewardship.

title: Divorce and Remarriage
question: When, if ever, may a Christian divorce and marry again?
common: Christians agree that God intends marriage to be a lifelong covenant ('What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder,' Matthew 19:6), and that divorce always involves real loss.

views.label: A true marriage is unbreakable
views.summary: A valid, consummated sacramental marriage cannot be dissolved by any human power, following Jesus' words in Mark 10:11-12. Spouses may separate for serious reasons but may not remarry while the other is living. The Church may grant a declaration of nullity (an annulment) when it finds that a true marriage never existed from the start.

views.label: Lifelong, with pastoral mercy
views.summary: The Orthodox Church upholds marriage as lifelong, yet out of pastoral mercy (called 'economy') it may allow a second and, rarely, a third marriage after divorce, for causes such as adultery. The service for a second marriage has a more penitential tone.

views.tradition: Many Lutheran, Reformed, Baptist, and other Protestants
views.label: For adultery or desertion
views.summary: Divorce is permitted when a spouse commits adultery (Matthew 19:9) or when an unbelieving spouse leaves (1 Corinthians 7:15), and the innocent party may remarry. The Westminster Confession holds this view. Many today also treat abuse as a form of breaking the marriage covenant.

views.label: No remarriage while spouse lives
views.summary: Remarriage after divorce is not permitted while a former spouse is alive, following Mark 10:11-12 and Luke 16:18, which give no exception. Matthew's 'except it be for fornication' is often understood to refer to unfaithfulness during betrothal, which Joseph thought had happened with Mary (Matthew 1:19).

note: Practice often varies by congregation, and many churches give particular pastoral care in cases of abuse.

title: How the Church Is Led
question: How should the church be led and organized?
common: Christians agree that Christ is 'the head of the body, the church' (Colossians 1:18), that leaders are to be servants and shepherds, and that the New Testament names elders and deacons.

views.label: Bishops united with the pope
views.summary: Christ gave authority to the apostles, who appointed successors, the bishops, who lead the Church with priests and deacons. Paul's charge to Titus to 'ordain elders in every city' (Titus 1:5) shows apostolic authority being handed on. The bishops serve in communion with the bishop of Rome.

views.label: Bishops gathered in councils
views.summary: The Church is led by bishops in succession from the apostles, each with priests and deacons, joined together in councils (synods) as in Acts 15. Each regional church governs itself, but all share one faith and communion, and no single bishop rules the whole Church.

views.label: Bishops, priests, and deacons
views.summary: Anglicans keep the threefold ministry of bishops, priests, and deacons, which their ordination services describe as present in the church 'from the Apostles' time.' Clergy and laity share in governing the church through synods.

views.label: Led by elders together
views.summary: Presbyterian and Reformed churches are governed by elders (presbyters), both teaching and ruling elders, who lead together. The New Testament uses 'elder' and 'bishop' (overseer) for the same office (Titus 1:5-7; Acts 20:17, 28). Congregations are joined in regional and national assemblies, following the pattern of the council in Acts 15.

views.tradition: Many Baptists and other congregational churches
views.label: The congregation decides
views.summary: Each local church governs itself under Christ, with members deciding key matters such as calling a pastor and church discipline (Matthew 18:17). Churches are usually led by pastors (elders) and deacons and cooperate freely with other churches, but no outside body has authority over them.

note: Some Lutheran and Methodist churches also have bishops, understanding the office in a variety of ways.

title: Asking the Saints to Pray
question: May Christians ask the saints in heaven to pray for them?
common: Christians agree that believers who have died are alive with God, for 'all live unto him' (Luke 20:38), and that it is good to ask fellow believers to pray for us (James 5:16).

views.label: Asking for their prayers
views.summary: Catholics ask the saints, especially Mary, to pray for them, just as they would ask a friend on earth. The saints are 'so great a cloud of witnesses' (Hebrews 12:1), and Revelation shows the elders in heaven offering 'the prayers of saints' to God (Revelation 5:8). Honor given to the saints is different from worship, which belongs to God alone.

views.label: One family in Christ
views.summary: Asking the saints for their prayers is part of everyday Orthodox life and worship, since in Christ death does not divide the Church. Honor (veneration) is given to the saints, while worship is given to God alone. Every prayer to a saint rests on Christ, the only Savior.

views.label: Honor them, pray to God
views.summary: The Lutheran Confessions honor the saints, give thanks for them, and teach that the saints in heaven pray for the church. But they do not call on the saints in prayer, because Scripture gives no command or promise for it, and Christ is the 'one mediator between God and men' (1 Timothy 2:5).

views.tradition: Many Reformed, Baptist, and other evangelicals
views.label: Pray to God alone
views.summary: Prayer is addressed to God alone, through Christ, who 'ever liveth to make intercession' for believers (Hebrews 7:25). Scripture gives no example of praying to departed believers, and many see the practice as risking honor that belongs only to God. The 'cloud of witnesses' in Hebrews 12 are examples of faith to follow.

note: Anglican practice varies widely: some Anglicans ask for the saints' prayers, and many do not.

title: Purgatory
question: Is there a final cleansing after death for those who are saved?
common: Christians agree that God is holy, that nothing unclean will enter his presence (Revelation 21:27), and that Christ's sacrifice is the only ground of salvation.

views.label: A final purification
views.summary: Those who die in God's grace but are not yet fully purified undergo a final cleansing, called purgatory, so they can enter the joy of heaven. It is not a second chance; all in purgatory are saved. Catholics see it in Paul's words that some 'shall be saved; yet so as by fire' (1 Corinthians 3:15) and in the Jewish practice of praying for the dead described in 2 Maccabees 12, a book outside the Protestant canon.

views.label: Prayer for the departed
views.summary: The Orthodox pray for the departed and believe those prayers help them, but they do not accept the Catholic teaching on purgatory as a place of purifying punishment. They speak of the time before the final judgment as a mystery, without defining it in detail.

views.label: With Christ at once
views.summary: At death believers, fully forgiven through Christ's finished work, go at once into the Lord's presence, 'absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord' (2 Corinthians 5:8). Jesus told the thief, 'To day shalt thou be with me in paradise' (Luke 23:43). 1 Corinthians 3:15 is read as the testing of a believer's works on judgment day, not a cleansing of the person.

note: Some Anglicans and Lutherans pray for the departed in general terms without affirming purgatory.

title: Which Books Are Scripture?
question: Which books belong in the Old Testament?
common: Christians agree on the 27 books of the New Testament and on the books of the Hebrew Bible, which every church includes in its Old Testament.

views.label: Deuterocanonical books included
views.summary: The Catholic Old Testament includes seven more books, called deuterocanonical: Tobit, Judith, 1 and 2 Maccabees, Wisdom, Sirach, and Baruch, plus longer forms of Esther and Daniel. These were part of the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint) widely used by the early church, were listed by councils in North Africa around AD 400, and were confirmed at the Council of Trent. Many church fathers quoted them as Scripture.

views.label: The fuller Greek Old Testament
views.summary: Orthodox Bibles include the books Catholics accept and several more from the Septuagint, such as 1 Esdras, 3 Maccabees, the Prayer of Manasseh, and Psalm 151. These are read in worship and valued as Scripture, though some Orthodox teachers rank them below the books of the Hebrew Bible.

views.label: Good to read, not doctrine
views.summary: These churches base doctrine on the books of the Hebrew Bible but keep the Apocrypha as worthwhile reading. The Anglican Thirty-nine Articles, following St. Jerome, say the church reads them 'for example of life and instruction of manners' but not 'to establish any doctrine' (Article VI). Luther's Bible printed them in a separate section between the Testaments.

views.label: Hebrew Bible only
views.summary: These churches accept only the 39 books of the Hebrew Bible, the Scriptures of the Jewish people, to whom 'were committed the oracles of God' (Romans 3:2). Jesus spoke of 'the law of Moses, and... the prophets, and... the psalms' (Luke 24:44), and the New Testament never directly cites the Apocrypha as Scripture. The Westminster Confession says these books are no part of the canon and are to be treated like other human writings.

note: The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church has a still larger canon, including 1 Enoch, which Jude 1:14-15 quotes.

title: Confession and Forgiveness
question: Should Christians confess their sins to a priest or pastor, or to God alone?
common: Christians agree that God freely forgives all who confess and repent ('If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us,' 1 John 1:9), and that believers should seek reconciliation with those they have wronged.

views.label: The sacrament of Reconciliation
views.summary: Jesus gave the apostles power to forgive sins: 'Whose soever sins ye remit, they are remitted unto them' (John 20:23). Catholics believe this continues in the sacrament of Penance, where the priest, acting in Christ's name, grants absolution. Confessing grave sins in this sacrament is required, it is encouraged for lesser sins, and what is said is protected by an absolute seal of secrecy.

views.label: Confession before Christ
views.summary: In Orthodox confession, the believer confesses to Christ in the presence of a priest, who acts as witness and spiritual guide and then prays the prayer of forgiveness. It is seen as healing for the soul more than a legal procedure. Confession is normally part of preparing for Holy Communion, though how often varies.

views.label: Private absolution kept
views.summary: Lutherans keep private confession and absolution, which the Augsburg Confession says should not be abolished, though listing every sin is not required. The pastor declares God's forgiveness by Christ's command, and Luther prized absolution as a great comfort. Lutheran worship also includes a general confession and absolution.

views.label: All may; none must
views.summary: The Book of Common Prayer provides for private confession to a priest with absolution, but it is not required. A common Anglican saying puts it this way: 'All may, none must, some should.' Regular services include a general confession and a declaration of God's forgiveness.

views.label: Directly to God through Christ
views.summary: Believers confess their sins directly to God, because Christ is their great high priest and every believer may 'come boldly unto the throne of grace' (Hebrews 4:16). James 5:16 is read as mutual confession among believers, not confession to clergy. John 20:23 is understood as authority to announce God's forgiveness through the gospel.

title: Growing in Holiness
question: How holy can a Christian become in this life?
common: Christians agree that God calls his people to holiness, that the Holy Spirit changes believers over time, and that when Christ appears 'we shall be like him' (1 John 3:2).

views.label: Perfect love is possible
views.summary: John Wesley taught that believers can, by God's grace, be made 'perfect in love' in this life, so that love for God and neighbor rules the heart and they no longer willfully sin. This 'Christian perfection' does not mean freedom from mistakes, weakness, or temptation. Wesleyans point to Jesus' call 'Be ye therefore perfect' (Matthew 5:48) and Paul's prayer that God would 'sanctify you wholly' (1 Thessalonians 5:23).

views.label: Growing, never finished here
views.summary: Sanctification is a lifelong work in which the Holy Spirit makes believers more like Christ, but it is never complete in this life. Even mature believers still struggle with sin, as Paul describes in Romans 7, and 'If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves' (1 John 1:8). 1 John 3:9 is read as describing the believer's settled direction, not a sinless life.

views.label: Saint and sinner at once
views.summary: A Christian is 'at the same time righteous and a sinner': fully righteous in Christ by faith, while still struggling with the sinful nature until death. Growth in love and good works is real, but believers always live by returning to God's grace in daily repentance.

views.label: Called to holiness
views.summary: Every Christian is called to holiness, and with God's grace real growth toward perfect love of God and neighbor is possible; the saints show what this looks like. Even holy people commit lesser (venial) sins, and complete purification is finished in heaven, through purgatory if needed. 'Follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord' (Hebrews 12:14).

views.label: Theosis: union with God
views.summary: The Orthodox describe salvation as theosis, becoming 'partakers of the divine nature' (2 Peter 1:4) by grace. Through prayer, the sacraments, and spiritual struggle, believers are healed and transformed, a journey that continues into eternity. Holy people are living icons of this change, yet even the greatest saints counted themselves sinners.

note: Holiness churches, such as the Church of the Nazarene, and some Pentecostal churches teach entire sanctification as a distinct work of grace.

title: Healing Today
question: How should churches pray for the sick, and does God promise healing?
common: Christians agree that God can heal, that praying for the sick is right and good (James 5:14-15), and that full healing of every sickness will come at the resurrection.

views.label: Healing provided in the cross
views.summary: Many Pentecostals teach that healing for the body is provided for in Christ's atoning work, since 'with his stripes we are healed' (Isaiah 53:5) and Matthew applies Isaiah's words to Jesus' healings (Matthew 8:17). Churches pray for the sick with anointing oil and the laying on of hands and expect God to heal, while recognizing that not everyone is healed in this life.

views.label: Anointing of the Sick
views.summary: James 5:14-15 is the basis for the sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick, in which a priest anoints the seriously ill or elderly with oil and prays over them. It gives strength, peace, and forgiveness of sins, and sometimes physical healing if that serves the person's salvation. The Church also recognizes miraculous healings after careful investigation.

views.label: Holy Unction
views.summary: The Orthodox celebrate the sacrament of Holy Unction, an anointing with prayer for the healing of body and soul, offered to the sick and, in many places, to all the faithful during Holy Week. They also seek healing through the prayers of the saints.

views.tradition: Many Reformed, Baptist, and other evangelicals
views.label: God heals as he wills
views.summary: God can and does heal in answer to prayer, and elders should pray for the sick as James instructs. But healing is not promised in every case in this life: Paul's 'thorn in the flesh' remained so that God's strength would be shown in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9), and he left Trophimus sick at Miletum (2 Timothy 4:20). Medical care is seen as one of God's good gifts.

note: Lutherans, Anglicans, and Methodists also have services of prayer and anointing for the sick.

title: When Little Ones Die
question: What happens to babies and young children who die?
common: Christians agree that God is just and merciful, that Jesus welcomed little children, and that any child's salvation rests on God's grace in Christ.

views.label: Entrusted to God's mercy
views.summary: The Church is certain of the salvation of baptized children who die. For children who die without baptism, the Church entrusts them to God's mercy and hopes for their salvation, recalling Jesus' words, 'Suffer the little children to come unto me' (Mark 10:14). The idea of 'limbo' was a theological opinion, never official Church teaching.

views.label: Innocent, in God's care
views.summary: The Orthodox do not believe infants carry personal guilt for Adam's sin, so children who die are not condemned for sins they did not commit. They are entrusted to God's love, and the Church's prayers for departed children express trust in his mercy.

views.label: Hope in God's grace
views.summary: Lutherans stress baptism as the ordinary means by which God gives faith to infants, but they do not teach that God is bound by it. Children who die before baptism are commended to God's mercy in hope.

views.label: Covenant hope for children
views.summary: The Canons of Dort teach that believing parents should not doubt the salvation of their children whom God calls out of this life in infancy, because of God's covenant promise. The Westminster Confession speaks of 'elect infants, dying in infancy' being saved by Christ through the Spirit. Many Reformed teachers extend this hope to all who die in infancy.

views.label: Safe with the Lord
views.summary: Children who die before they can understand right and wrong go to be with the Lord. David said of his infant son, 'I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me' (2 Samuel 12:23), and God spoke of children who 'had no knowledge between good and evil' (Deuteronomy 1:39). This is often called the 'age of accountability.'

title: The Antichrist
question: Who is the 'man of sin,' and is the Antichrist a person still to come?
common: Christians agree that opposition to Christ has been at work since the apostles' time ('even now are there many antichrists,' 1 John 2:18) and that Christ will finally defeat all evil (2 Thessalonians 2:8).

views.label: A final deception
views.summary: Before Christ's return a final trial will shake the faith of many, in the form of a religious deception that offers people an apparent answer to their problems at the price of abandoning the truth. Many Catholic teachers, following the church fathers, expect a personal Antichrist at the end, though the Church has not defined the details.

views.label: Final person, present spirit
views.summary: Following church fathers such as St. Cyril of Jerusalem and St. John Chrysostom, the Orthodox expect a personal Antichrist at the end of the age. They also stress that the spirit of antichrist is already at work wherever Christ is denied (1 John 4:3).

views.label: A coming world ruler
views.summary: A future political ruler will make a covenant with Israel, then break it and set himself up in a rebuilt temple during the tribulation (Daniel 9:27; 2 Thessalonians 2:4). The one who now 'letteth,' or restrains, him (2 Thessalonians 2:7) is often identified as the Holy Spirit working through the church, removed at the rapture.

views.label: A corruption within the church
views.summary: The Reformers read the 'man of sin' who 'sitteth in the temple of God' (2 Thessalonians 2:4) as a false authority arising inside the church rather than outside it, and the Lutheran and Westminster confessions identified it with the office of the papacy. Many Lutheran and Reformed Christians today no longer hold this view or hold it only about the office, not individual popes, and many also expect a final personal Antichrist.

note: Some interpreters across traditions read 2 Thessalonians 2 as mainly fulfilled in events around the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70.

title: Daniel's Seventy Weeks
question: What do Daniel's seventy weeks point to, and is the last week still to come?
common: Christians agree that Daniel 9 is a prophecy of God's plan 'to make reconciliation for iniquity, and to bring in everlasting righteousness' (Daniel 9:24), and most see it pointing to the Messiah.

views.label: A gap before week seventy
views.summary: The seventy 'weeks' are 490 years. The first 69 weeks ended in Jesus' time, when 'Messiah' was 'cut off' (Daniel 9:26). Then God paused the prophetic clock for the church age, and the seventieth week is a future seven-year tribulation, when a coming ruler will make and then break a covenant with Israel (Daniel 9:27).

views.label: Fulfilled in Christ
views.summary: All seventy weeks run in sequence to Christ's first coming. The one who 'shall confirm the covenant with many' and 'cause the sacrifice and the oblation to cease' (Daniel 9:27) is Christ, whose death established the new covenant and ended the need for temple sacrifices. The destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 followed, as Jesus foretold (Luke 21:20).

views.label: Messianic, read with the fathers
views.summary: Many church fathers saw the weeks fulfilled in Christ's death and the end of the temple sacrifices, and this reading is common in Catholic and Orthodox tradition. Many modern Catholic scholars also see the passage speaking to the crisis under the Greek king Antiochus IV in the 160s BC, described in Daniel's later chapters, while seeing its fullest meaning in Christ.

note: Interpreters also differ on the starting date of the seventy weeks and on how to count the years.

title: The Old Testament Law Today
question: Which Old Testament laws do Christians still keep?
common: Christians agree that Jesus fulfilled the law, that the sacrifices are completed in his death, and that loving God and neighbor sums up the law (Matthew 22:37-40).

views.label: The moral law abides
views.summary: The law has moral, ceremonial, and civil parts. The ceremonial laws, such as sacrifices and food laws, pointed to Christ and are fulfilled; the civil laws governed Israel as a nation; the moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments, still guides Christian life. Christ said, 'I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil' (Matthew 5:17).

views.label: Law and gospel
views.summary: Lutherans read all Scripture through the distinction between law and gospel. The law shows our sin and drives us to Christ, and it also guides believers' lives, but it can never save. Christ is 'the end of the law for righteousness to every one that believeth' (Romans 10:4).

views.label: Old Law fulfilled
views.summary: The Old Law prepared the way for the gospel. Its moral teaching, summed up in the Ten Commandments, remains, while its ceremonial and judicial rules were fulfilled in Christ. The New Law is the grace of the Holy Spirit given through faith in Christ, working through love.

views.label: The law of Christ
views.summary: The law of Moses was given to Israel as a whole and ended as a rule of life at the cross, for 'we are no longer under a schoolmaster' (Galatians 3:25). Christians live under 'the law of Christ' (Galatians 6:2), and Old Testament commands repeated in the New Testament, such as nine of the Ten Commandments, still apply.

views.label: Read through Jesus' teaching
views.summary: The Old Testament is read through Jesus, especially the Sermon on the Mount, where he says 'Ye have heard that it hath been said... But I say unto you' (Matthew 5:38-39). Christ's teaching completes the old law and, on matters such as oaths and violence, calls his followers beyond it.

title: War and Nonviolence
question: May Christians use force, serve in war, or defend themselves?
common: Christians agree that Jesus calls his followers to love their enemies, to be peacemakers (Matthew 5:9), and never to take personal revenge (Romans 12:19).

views.label: Nonresistance and peace
views.summary: Jesus' commands to 'resist not evil' and to 'Love your enemies' (Matthew 5:39, 44) apply fully to Christians, so believers should not kill, even in war. Christ's kingdom 'is not of this world' and does not advance by the sword (John 18:36), and many early Christian writers taught against taking life. Many Anabaptists serve instead through relief work and peacemaking.

views.label: Just war, peace first
views.summary: Governments may use force to defend people against unjust aggression, but only under strict conditions, including a just cause, last resort, a real chance of success, and force proportionate to the harm. This 'just war' tradition, developed by St. Augustine and St. Thomas Aquinas, draws on the ruler's role to bear 'the sword' (Romans 13:4). Recent popes have stressed how rarely modern war can meet these conditions, and the Church respects conscientious objectors.

views.label: War as a tragic necessity
views.summary: The Orthodox Church honors soldiers who defend their people, and some are counted among the saints, but it has never developed a formal just war theory and treats all killing as tragic. In early church practice, St. Basil advised that even soldiers who killed in war refrain from Communion for a time.

views.label: Just war permitted
views.summary: Christians may serve as soldiers and police, for when soldiers asked John the Baptist what to do, he told them to 'Do violence to no man... and be content with your wages,' not to leave the army (Luke 3:14). The Augsburg Confession says Christians may 'engage in just wars.' Jesus' words in Matthew 5 govern personal revenge, while the state is God's servant to restrain evil (Romans 13:4).

note: Quakers and some Methodists, Baptists, and Pentecostals also hold to nonviolence; several early Pentecostal denominations were pacifist.

title: Receiving the Holy Spirit
question: Is there an experience of the Holy Spirit after conversion?
common: Christians agree that every believer has the Holy Spirit (Romans 8:9) and that believers should seek to be 'filled with the Spirit' (Ephesians 5:18).

views.label: A later gift of power
views.summary: Baptism in the Holy Spirit is a distinct experience after salvation that gives power for witness (Acts 1:8). In Acts 8 the Samaritans believed and were baptized but received the Spirit only later when the apostles laid hands on them, and in Acts 19 Paul asked believers, 'Have ye received the Holy Ghost since ye believed?' Pentecostals see speaking in tongues as its first outward sign.

views.label: The sacrament of Confirmation
views.summary: Catholics see in Acts 8:14-17 the roots of the sacrament of Confirmation, in which the bishop, or a priest he authorizes, lays on hands and anoints the baptized so they receive the strength of the Holy Spirit to live and witness to the faith. Many Catholics also speak of a renewal or 'release' of the Spirit already received.

views.label: Chrismation with baptism
views.summary: The Orthodox give the gift of the Holy Spirit through chrismation, an anointing with holy oil immediately after baptism, even for infants, with the words 'The seal of the gift of the Holy Spirit.' A lifelong growth in the Spirit is then the aim of all Christian living.

views.tradition: Many Reformed, Baptist, and other evangelicals
views.label: Received at conversion
views.summary: Every believer is baptized in the Spirit at conversion: 'by one Spirit are we all baptized into one body' (1 Corinthians 12:13). The events in Acts 8, 10, and 19 are seen as special moments as the gospel reached new groups (Samaritans, Gentiles, and followers of John the Baptist), showing they belonged to the one church. Believers may have many later fillings of the Spirit.

note: Anglicans and Lutherans also practice confirmation, often understood as affirming baptismal vows with prayer for the Spirit's strengthening. Wesleyan-Holiness churches have taught a 'second blessing' linked with entire sanctification.

title: Assurance of Salvation
question: Can a person know for sure that they are saved?
common: Christians agree that believers can have real confidence in God's promises and love, and that this hope rests on Christ, not on their own goodness.

views.label: Real assurance, often grown into
views.summary: True believers can be certainly assured that they are in a state of grace, based on God's promises, the inner witness of the Spirit (Romans 8:16), and the fruit of a changed life. But assurance is not the essence of faith, and a true believer may struggle for a long time before having it, as the Westminster Confession teaches. John wrote 'that ye may know that ye have eternal life' (1 John 5:13).

views.label: Know it by God's promise
views.summary: Anyone who has trusted Christ can know with certainty that they have eternal life, because God's Word says so: 'He that heareth my word, and believeth on him that sent me, hath everlasting life' (John 5:24). Doubts are answered by looking to Christ's finished work, not to one's feelings.

views.label: Look to the promise
views.summary: Assurance is grounded outside ourselves, in God's promise given in the Word, in baptism, and in the Lord's Supper. A troubled conscience is pointed not to its own feelings or works but to Christ's words, 'given for you.'

views.label: The witness of the Spirit
views.summary: Wesley taught that believers can know they are God's children through 'the witness of the Spirit,' the Spirit bearing witness 'with our spirit, that we are the children of God' (Romans 8:16), confirmed by the fruit of the Spirit. This is assurance of present salvation; because grace can be refused, it is not a guarantee apart from continuing faith.

views.label: Confident hope
views.summary: Catholics are called to a firm, confident hope in God's mercy and promises. But the Council of Trent taught that, without a special revelation from God, no one can be absolutely certain of persevering to the end, so believers 'work out' their salvation 'with fear and trembling' (Philippians 2:12) while trusting God, who began the good work, to complete it (Philippians 1:6).

views.label: Hope without presumption
views.summary: The Orthodox speak of salvation as a journey and are cautious about claiming certainty of the end, seeing that as presumption, while living in strong hope in God's love. A common Orthodox way of putting it is, 'I have been saved, I am being saved, and I hope to be saved.'

title: How to Read Revelation
question: Is Revelation about the first century, the whole church age, or the end of history?
common: Christians agree that Revelation reveals Jesus Christ as Lord over history, calls believers to faithfulness, and ends with God making 'all things new' (Revelation 21:5).

views.label: Futurist
views.summary: Most of Revelation, from chapter 4 on, describes events still to come: the tribulation, the Antichrist, Christ's return, and the millennium. Revelation 1:19 is read as an outline: what John had seen, 'the things which are,' and 'the things which shall be hereafter.'

views.label: Preterist
views.summary: Much of Revelation was fulfilled in the first century, especially in the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70 or in persecution under Rome. Preterists stress that John wrote of things which 'must shortly come to pass' and that 'the time is at hand' (Revelation 1:1, 3). Most still expect Christ's future return and final judgment.

views.label: Historicist
