views.summary: Many Reformers and later Protestants read Revelation as a panorama of history from the apostles to the end, matching its symbols to events in the history of the church and the world. This view was dominant among Protestants for several centuries.

views.label: Symbolic of every age
views.summary: Many readers see Revelation mainly as a symbolic picture of the ongoing struggle between Christ and evil in every age, ending in Christ's final victory, often combined with a first-century setting and a future fulfillment. Its scenes of heavenly worship have shaped Christian worship. The Orthodox honor Revelation as Scripture but do not read it in their regular public services.

note: Many interpreters blend these approaches, finding both first-century meaning and future fulfillment.

title: Original Sin
question: What did Adam's sin pass on to the rest of humanity?
common: Christians agree that sin and death entered the world through Adam (Romans 5:12), that every person needs God's grace, and that Christ brings life: 'as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive' (1 Corinthians 15:22).

views.label: A wounded nature
views.summary: Every person inherits original sin, the loss of the original holiness and justice God gave the first humans; it is 'contracted, not committed,' so it is not a personal fault. Human nature is wounded and inclined to sin, but not totally corrupted. Baptism removes original sin, though the inclination to sin remains as a struggle.

views.label: Inherited mortality, not guilt
views.summary: Orthodox teachers usually speak of 'ancestral sin': everyone inherits the results of Adam's fall, especially death and corruption, but not Adam's personal guilt, since 'the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father' (Ezekiel 18:20). Many Orthodox read Romans 5:12 to mean that death spread to all, and because of death all sin.

views.label: Inherited guilt and corruption
views.summary: Adam acted as the head of the human race, so all people inherit both his guilt and a corrupted nature. This does not mean people are as bad as they could be, but that sin affects every part of a person, including mind and will; Reformed Christians call this 'total depravity.' David said, 'in sin did my mother conceive me' (Psalms 51:5), and Paul says we 'were by nature the children of wrath' (Ephesians 2:3).

views.label: Fallen, but grace reaches all
views.summary: Wesleyans firmly affirm original sin: human nature is deeply corrupted by Adam's fall. But they teach that grace, given through Christ to every person, partly restores the ability to respond to God, and many hold that the guilt of Adam's sin is removed for all through Christ's death, 'the free gift came upon all men' (Romans 5:18).

title: Icons and Images
question: Is it right to use images of Christ and the saints in worship?
common: Christians agree that worship belongs to God alone and that idolatry is forbidden. They also note that God commanded some images in Israel's worship, such as the cherubim over the ark (Exodus 25:18).

views.label: Icons honor the incarnation
views.summary: Because God the Son became man and was seen ('the Word was made flesh,' John 1:14), he can be pictured; Christ is 'the image of the invisible God' (Colossians 1:15). Orthodox Christians venerate icons by kissing them and lighting candles before them, but worship God alone; as the Seventh Ecumenical Council (787) taught, the honor passes to the person shown. Icons are often called windows into heaven.

views.label: Sacred images honored
views.summary: Catholics accept the teaching of the Second Council of Nicaea (787) that sacred images may be honored, because the honor given to an image passes to the person it represents. Crucifixes, statues, and paintings help the faithful remember and love Christ and the saints, but adoration belongs to God alone.

views.label: Images allowed, not venerated
views.summary: Luther defended keeping crucifixes, altar paintings, and other images as helpful for teaching and devotion, against those who wanted them destroyed. Lutherans do not venerate images, but treat them as a Christian freedom so long as they are not trusted in or worshiped.

views.label: No images in worship
views.summary: Many Reformed churches understand the second commandment to forbid not only worshiping images but also using images of God in worship, including pictures of Christ. When God spoke to Israel, they 'saw no manner of similitude' (Deuteronomy 4:15), and Hezekiah destroyed even the bronze serpent once it was misused (2 Kings 18:4). Reformed churches therefore tend to have plain sanctuaries centered on the pulpit, table, and font.

note: Anglicans, Methodists, and Baptists vary widely; many use crosses, stained glass, and artwork without venerating them.

title: How Many Sacraments?
question: How many sacraments are there, and what makes something a sacrament?
common: Nearly all Christians agree that Christ commanded baptism and the Lord's Supper and that his church should celebrate them until he returns.

views.label: Seven sacraments
views.summary: There are seven sacraments instituted by Christ: Baptism, Confirmation, the Eucharist, Penance, Anointing of the Sick, Holy Orders, and Matrimony. A sacrament is an effective sign of grace through which Christ himself acts to give the grace it signifies. Paul calls marriage 'a great mystery' pointing to Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:32), and the Latin Bible translated 'mystery' as sacramentum.

views.label: The Holy Mysteries
views.summary: The Orthodox speak of 'Holy Mysteries' and commonly list the same seven, though they do not limit God's grace to a fixed number; services such as the great blessing of water are also seen as sacred. Through the mysteries the Holy Spirit unites people to Christ.

views.label: Two, sometimes three
views.summary: Baptism and the Lord's Supper are sacraments because each has Christ's command, a visible element, and a promise of forgiveness. The Lutheran Confessions also call absolution a sacrament. Other rites, such as marriage and ordination, are holy but are not means of forgiveness in the same way.

views.label: Two sacraments of the gospel
views.summary: There are two sacraments ordained by Christ in the gospel, Baptism and the Lord's Supper, which are signs and seals of God's grace. The Anglican Articles call the other five 'commonly called Sacraments' but not 'Sacraments of the Gospel' (Article XXV).

views.label: Two ordinances
views.summary: Baptists usually speak of two 'ordinances,' Baptism and the Lord's Supper, stressing that they are acts of obedience Christ ordered his church to do. They are rich signs and occasions of blessing, but they do not themselves give saving grace.

note: Some Anabaptist, Baptist, and other churches also practice foot washing as an ordinance, following John 13:14-15.

title: Who May Receive Communion?
question: Who may come to the Lord's Supper?
common: Christians agree that the Lord's Supper is holy, that it should be received with faith and self-examination ('let a man examine himself,' 1 Corinthians 11:28), and that it expresses unity in Christ.

views.label: A sign of full unity
views.summary: Because receiving the Eucharist expresses full unity in faith with the Church, Catholics generally receive only within the Catholic Church, and other Christians are normally asked not to receive. Catholics should first confess any grave sin, mindful of Paul's warning about eating 'unworthily' (1 Corinthians 11:27). Limited exceptions exist, especially for Orthodox Christians.

views.label: For Orthodox who are prepared
views.summary: Holy Communion is given to baptized Orthodox Christians who have prepared through prayer, fasting, and usually confession. Receiving together expresses one shared faith, so the Orthodox do not share Communion with other churches.

views.label: Close to fully open
views.summary: Many confessional Lutherans, such as the Lutheran Church–Missouri Synod, practice 'close' Communion for those who share their confession, especially about Christ's real presence, citing Paul's warning about 'not discerning the Lord's body' (1 Corinthians 11:29). Other Lutheran churches, such as the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America, invite all baptized Christians.

views.tradition: Many Methodists, Anglicans, Reformed, and evangelicals
views.label: Open to all believers
views.summary: Many Protestant churches welcome all baptized believers, or all who trust in Christ, to the table, seeing it as the Lord's table rather than a denomination's. Methodists practice an especially open table, following John Wesley's view that the Supper is a means of grace that can even help bring people to faith.

note: Some Baptist churches limit the Supper to baptized members of that church or of like faith, while many others welcome all believers.

title: Married or Celibate Clergy
question: Should priests and pastors be married or celibate?
common: Christians agree that both marriage and singleness are good gifts from God (1 Corinthians 7:7), and that the apostle Peter was married (Matthew 8:14).

views.label: Celibacy for ministry
views.summary: In the Latin (Western) Church, priests are normally chosen from men who commit to celibacy, following Christ's own life and Paul's teaching that the unmarried can care for 'the things that belong to the Lord' (1 Corinthians 7:32). This is a discipline, not a doctrine: Eastern Catholic churches have married priests, some married former Protestant clergy are ordained, and married men may become permanent deacons.

views.label: Married priests, celibate bishops
views.summary: Orthodox priests may be married if they marry before ordination, and many are. Bishops are chosen from celibate clergy, usually monks. Monastic celibacy is honored as a high calling.

views.tradition: Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican, and other Protestants
views.label: Free to marry
views.summary: The Reformers taught that ministers are free to marry, since Paul expects an overseer to be 'the husband of one wife' (1 Timothy 3:2) and the apostles had wives (1 Corinthians 9:5). Luther himself married, and most Protestant pastors are married, while singleness is honored as a gift.

title: Taking Oaths
question: May Christians take oaths, such as in court?
common: Christians agree that believers must always speak the truth, letting their 'yea be yea; and your nay, nay' (James 5:12).

views.label: Swear not at all
views.summary: Anabaptists take Jesus' words 'Swear not at all' (Matthew 5:34) and James 5:12 as a direct command, so they decline to take oaths, even in court, and instead solemnly affirm that they are telling the truth. A Christian's every word should be as true as an oath.

views.label: Oaths for serious reasons
views.summary: Oaths are allowed when made truthfully and for serious reasons, such as in court, since God himself confirmed his promise with an oath (Hebrews 6:17) and Paul called God as his witness (Romans 1:9). Jesus forbids careless or false swearing, not every solemn oath.

views.tradition: Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican, and many evangelicals
views.label: Lawful oaths permitted
views.summary: The Reformation confessions, including the Augsburg Confession, the Westminster Confession, and the Anglican Articles, teach that Christians may take lawful oaths when a magistrate requires them. They read Jesus as forbidding casual and evasive oaths, which some in his day used to dodge the truth (Matthew 23:16-22).

note: Quakers and some Baptists and other evangelicals also prefer to affirm rather than swear.

title: Christians and Government
question: How should Christians relate to government and political power?
common: Christians agree they should pray for rulers (1 Timothy 2:1-2), obey just laws, and 'Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's' (Matthew 22:21), and that 'We ought to obey God rather than men' (Acts 5:29) when the two conflict.

views.label: Two kingdoms
views.summary: God rules the world in two ways: through the gospel in the church, and through law and government in society, which is 'the minister of God to thee for good' (Romans 13:4). Christians can serve fully as citizens and officials, but the church should not wield the sword, and government should not command the gospel.

views.label: Christ is Lord of all
views.summary: Christ is Lord over every part of life, including government. Rulers are accountable to God's moral law, and Christians are called to work for justice in public life. Reformed thinkers helped develop ideas such as limits on rulers' power and resisting tyranny through lawful authorities.

views.label: A separate, peaceable people
views.summary: Christ's kingdom 'is not of this world' (John 18:36), so the church is a distinct community that does not rely on government power. Christians respect and pray for authorities and pay taxes, but many Anabaptists do not hold offices that require using force. The Schleitheim Confession (1527) said the sword is 'ordained of God outside the perfection of Christ.'

views.label: Distinct, serving the common good
views.summary: Church and state are distinct, each with its own role, but they should work together for the common good. Catholic social teaching holds that government exists to serve human dignity and the common good, and the Second Vatican Council taught that every person has a right to religious freedom.

views.label: Harmony of church and state
views.summary: Orthodox tradition, shaped in the Byzantine Empire, speaks of 'symphony,' a harmony in which church and state each serve God in their own sphere. Today Orthodox churches live under many kinds of governments and stress the church's freedom to carry out its spiritual mission.

note: Baptists have historically been strong advocates of religious liberty and the separation of church and state.
